rows: Scorpions can apparently see 360 degrees around the body, because the two median eyes and the side eyes together cover the circle.

Recordings from the eyes of two scorpion genera show the strongest response to blue light near 470 nm and to green light near 525 nm. Other work puts the main peak of scorpion eyes near 500 nm in green.
Scorpions are nocturnal and hide by day. Their eyes are sensitive to starlight levels of light.
The two median eyes are the main eyes and give relatively good detail for such small eyes. The side eyes seem to detect only changes in brightness.

Sand scorpions sense the footsteps of prey through slit organs in their legs from as far as 50 cm away. A courting male Centruroides margaritatus shakes in pulses about 0.018 s long, about 0.028 s apart.

No record gives how sharp a scorpion's picture is, so this view assumes coarse shapes. The size of the brightness boost, the mix of the two colour channels, the buzz in the rhythm of the judder and the pulse at the picture's edge are the app's.
A scorpion also finds food and mates by taste and touch through its comb-like pectines, and the camera records neither.

rows: A bottlenose dolphin has no short-wave cone, so it lacks the common colour sense of most land mammals. Whales and seals have only one kind of cone. We show the picture almost without colour.

A Bryde's whale resolves about 4.8 cycles per degree in water, a humpback about 3.3. A harbour seal, underwater, about 11.5. We set the picture at 3.3, the humpback figure, close to the cetacean values.
A bottlenose dolphin sees a panoramic field of 120 to 130 degrees, with its two eyes overlapping only 20 to 30 degrees. We widen the picture to match.
Dolphins and some whales have a reflective blue-green layer behind the retina. A harbour seal's retina is well developed for low light. We add a faint glow to moving things and a sheen.
The sharp middle, the dim-light gain, the glow colour and the fading of still things are the app's own choices. No record gives them, so we set them by eye.

rows: A honeybee resolves gratings of about a quarter of a cycle per degree, roughly one two-hundredth of a person's sharpness. Bumblebees and stingless bees fall in the same range.

Bees have three colour receptors, peaking in the ultraviolet near 340 to 350 nanometres, in the blue near 440 nanometres and in the green near 540 nanometres. The view shows the ultraviolet as blue, the blue as green and the green as red, so the picture is not a true colour match.
A bee sees almost all around itself, about 300 degrees across the horizontal. The picture is squeezed toward this wide field.
Bees hold their gaze still between quick head turns that last about 45 to 135 milliseconds. The view jumps in short steps to show this.
The sharpness, the glow of movement, the slow pace and the palette of this view are the app's own choices. The records give the bee's limits, but not how they look on a screen.

rows: Macaques have three kinds of cone, most sensitive near 430, 531 and 561 nanometres, much like the three you have. Baboons, apes and howler monkeys also see with three. We draw the colours with three sensors that sit close to yours.

Owl monkeys have a single type of cone and lack colour vision, as bushbabies do. Male marmosets have two kinds of cone. This view shows the three-cone case, so for those animals the colour is richer than the real thing.

A stumptail macaque resolves a gap of 1.4 minutes of arc, close to a person. Young rhesus monkeys reach 26.3 cycles per degree. A mouse lemur manages only about 4 to 5. We blur the picture to 24, near the macaque values.
A model of a chimpanzee-like eye socket lets each eye see out to 115 degrees to the side, against 136 degrees for a human. We narrow the picture by the same proportion.

Macaques, squirrel monkeys and marmosets have a clear fovea, a small pit of sharp vision. The owl monkey has only a rudimentary one. The records give no size for it, so the sharp middle is left as yours.
Most monkeys and apes are active by day. Owl monkeys and mouse lemurs are active at night. The records give no brightness ratio for them, so we leave brightness as yours.
The colour matrix, the single sharpness value for many species and the width of the field are the app's choices. They rest on the measurements above but are worked out or averaged by the app.

rows: An octopus resolves about 12 cycles per degree and a squid about 6.6, against your 30. A cuttlefish is put near 8. Newly hatched squid see far coarser, near 0.6. The picture is blurred to 8, a middle value that no single species is said to match.

Almost every octopus, squid and cuttlefish has one visual pigment, with its peak between 470 and 500 nanometres. An Octopus tetricus is described as colour-blind, and a cuttlefish retina cannot respond to colour. Cuttlefish cannot see red light. The picture loses its colour and keeps a brightness that favours blue-green.

Young oval squid take in about 312 degrees around them. One cuttlefish eye covers about 253 degrees, and the two eyes overlap by 86 degrees in front. Octopuses have no significant overlap. The camera holds a slice of this field and the rest is invented.
An octopus pupil is round in the dark and closes to a horizontal slit in bright light. Cuttlefish and Eledone can shrink theirs to 3% of the full area. The picture uses the horizontal slit.

Octopus photoreceptors crowd into a central horizontal stripe, about 55,000 per square millimetre against 18,000 to 22,000 at the edge. Squid and cuttlefish have a similar streak. The picture is sharper along a horizontal band, and how much sharper is the app's choice.

A squid loses flicker near 51 flashes a second, a cuttlefish near 30, and an octopus between 20 and 72 depending on the light. You lose it near 60. Squid time runs a little slower than yours and cuttlefish time at about half.

Octopuses respond to polarized light at a very fine threshold, a median of 0.010 on the polarization distance scale. The cephalopod retina has two sensitive planes, one horizontal and one vertical. The picture can show an overlay of where polarized light would stand out, and its look is the app's.

The single value of 8 cycles per degree, the 312 degree field taken from young squid, the strength of the sharp streak, the pace of 0.85, the horizontal pupil, the one-pigment colour matrix and the polarization overlay are the app's own settings, set inside the measured range.

Bees have three kinds of colour receptor. They peak near 346 nm in the ultraviolet, 430 nm in blue and 540 nm in green. Bees see ultraviolet light but cannot see far red.
In bright light a honeybee can still tell a flicker apart at about 200 flashes a second. A bumblebee manages about 130.
A strip of ommatidia along the top rim of the eye reads the pattern of polarised light in the sky. Bees use it as a compass. The app draws this pattern as an overlay.

rows: Two colours in the front eyes
The principal eyes of Saitis barbipes carry an ultraviolet pigment and a green pigment, peaking near 359 nm and 526 nm. No red receptor was found, so red and black look much alike to this view.

The front eyes of Portia fimbriata resolve about 12.4 cycles per degree, close to a bird of prey. Most salticids are far less sharp, so this picture is drawn at the sharpness of the best measured case.
Each principal retina is a thin upright strip, about 2 degrees wide and 21 degrees high in Phidippus johnsoni. Only that strip is sharp at once, and the eye moves it back and forth across the scene.
The side eyes of salticids together see almost all the way round, about 300 to 360 degrees, and they respond to movement. A person sees about 180 degrees.

The side eyes of Menemerus semilimbatus respond to moving targets and show a clear peak in turning near 50 degrees from straight ahead. Stationary targets never start a turn, which is why still things fade in this picture.
The brightness, the fading of still things, the lingering of the picture and the way sharpness falls with dim light are the app's own choices, set from the records but not measured in one animal.

The matrix uses the UV peak at 359 nm and the green peak at 526 nm measured in Saitis barbipes.

rows: Bottlenose dolphins have one kind of cone, most sensitive near 524 nanometres, and every whale and seal studied lacks the cone for blue. We pass the picture through that single sensor, so it loses its hues and turns grey.

Estimates of sharpness run from 1.6 cycles per degree in a manatee and 2.6 to 3.3 in small whales and porpoises, to 3.3 in a humpback whale and 4.8 in a Bryde's whale, and up to 11.5 in a harbour seal under water. You resolve about 30. We blur the picture to about 4, the middle of the two baleen whale estimates.

A bottlenose dolphin and a sperm whale are each recorded with a visual field of 120 to 130 degrees, and a dolphin's two eyes overlap by only 20 to 30 degrees. We narrow the picture to 125 degrees, the middle of that range.

A bottlenose dolphin saw 0.5 log units better than a person in dim light, which is about three times, and 0.2 log units worse in bright light. A reflective layer behind the retina is recorded in dolphins and in harbour seals, but manatees have none. We lift the dim picture about three times and add a faint sheen.

Manatees have two kinds of cone, so their colour sense may be richer than a dolphin's. A trained California sea lion could pick out colours in tests, though other work suggests it may have judged by brightness. A trained harbour seal behaved as colour-blind.
Dolphins find objects with clicks between 40 and 150 kilohertz, and a harbour seal can sense targets as far as 180 metres away with its whiskers. A phone can do neither, so this view leaves them out.

The sharpness of about 4 cycles per degree, the 125 degree field, the one-sensor colour mapping, the threefold brightness lift and the strength of the sheen are the app's own mappings of the records above. No record gave a pupil shape, so none is drawn.

rows: Many monkeys and apes have three kinds of cone, peaking near 561, 539 and 430 nanometres in the records we have. Owl monkeys have only one, so they see no colour at all.

A marmoset's cone mosaic is set up for about 30 cycles per degree at the centre. Measured neurons and behaviour in other monkeys give figures from about 5 to 26. We keep the middle sharp and blur the edges.
Owl monkeys are nocturnal and have only a rudimentary fovea, so their picture is dimmer and less sharp at the centre.
Infant monkeys and chimpanzee orbits suggest a wide sweep of view, but no field was measured for the whole animal. We keep a person's width.
The sharp middle, the overall width and the brightness are the app's own choices, as no record gives them for the whole animal.

rows: A scorpion's median and lateral eyes together give a view of all round its body, which is why the picture reaches all the way round.
Scorpion eyes peak in the blue-green, with a green peak at 525 nm in one set of species and a blue peak at 470 nm in another, so the picture leans blue-green.
The lateral eyes have a secondary ultraviolet sensitivity, and scorpions are attracted to 399 nm light at night, so the picture gives ultraviolet a small share.
Scorpions have a few large sensory eyes that respond to very low light, so the dark picture is brighter than the day picture.
Scorpions read the world mostly through their legs, pedipalps and pectines, which the camera does not record.
How sharp the picture is, how fast it blurs in dim light, how much still things fade, and the palette's greying are the app's guesses, since no record gives them.
